chapters.1: God commands Moses to take a census of all Israelite men twenty years and older who are able to fight, organized tribe by tribe, resulting in a total of 603,550 fighting men. The tribe of Levi is deliberately left out of this count because they are instead assigned to care for and camp around the tabernacle.
chapters.2: This chapter lays out the specific arrangement for Israel's camp, assigning each of the twelve tribes a position on one of four sides around the central tabernacle, with the Levites camped immediately around it. It also records each tribe's population total and the order tribes will travel in when the camp moves.
chapters.3: This chapter counts the Levites by their three clans—Gershon, Kohath, and Merari—and assigns each clan specific duties for transporting and caring for parts of the tabernacle. It also explains that the Levites formally take the place of Israel's firstborn sons, who technically belonged to God, with a redemption payment collected for the extra firstborn beyond the number of Levites.
chapters.4: This chapter details the specific tabernacle-carrying duties assigned to the Levite clans of Kohath, Gershon, and Merari, all for men aged thirty to fifty, with Kohath handling the holiest furnishings (carefully covered first so they don't look directly at them) and the others handling structural pieces and coverings. It concludes with the actual count of men in each clan eligible for this service.
chapters.5: This chapter covers the law of restitution for wrongs committed against another person, and the unusual "trial by ordeal" ritual for a wife suspected of unfaithfulness when there is no proof, in which she drinks a specially prepared water that is believed to bring consequences on her only if she is guilty.
chapters.6: This chapter describes the Nazarite vow, a temporary vow of special devotion in which a person abstains from wine, avoids cutting their hair, and avoids contact with dead bodies, along with the offerings required to complete the vow. It ends with the well-known priestly blessing Aaron and his sons are to pronounce over the people.
chapters.7: The leaders of each tribe bring generous dedication offerings for the newly completed tabernacle, including wagons and oxen for transport and identical sets of silver, gold, and sacrificial animals presented by each tribal leader over twelve consecutive days. The chapter closes by noting that God began speaking to Moses from above the ark's mercy seat.
chapters.8: This chapter describes the lighting of the golden lampstand and the ceremony for setting apart the Levites for tabernacle service, which includes purification rituals and the community symbolically laying hands on them. It also specifies that Levites serve from ages twenty-five to fifty, after which they still assist but no longer carry out full duties.
chapters.9: Israel observes the Passover in the wilderness of Sinai exactly as commanded, with provisions made for anyone ceremonially unclean or traveling to observe it a month later instead. The chapter closes by describing how the cloud of God's presence over the tabernacle directed Israel's movements, with the people traveling or staying camped depending on whether the cloud moved or stayed still.
chapters.10: God instructs Moses to make two silver trumpets to signal the people for assembly, travel, or war. The Israelites then set out from Sinai in their assigned marching order, guided by the cloud and the ark, with Moses inviting his brother-in-law Hobab along for his wilderness knowledge and declaring a traveling prayer whenever the ark set out or came to rest.
chapters.11: The people complain about hardship and crave the food they had in Egypt, growing tired of manna, which angers God and overwhelms Moses, so God has him appoint seventy elders to help share the burden of leadership. God also sends a huge quantity of quail to satisfy the people's craving for meat, but then strikes many of them with a plague for their greedy complaining.
chapters.12: Miriam and Aaron criticize Moses, partly over his marriage to a Cushite (Ethiopian) woman and partly out of jealousy over his unique relationship with God, prompting God to affirm Moses' unmatched standing as his prophet. As a result, Miriam is struck with a skin disease and temporarily excluded from the camp until Moses intercedes and she is healed.
chapters.13: Moses sends twelve spies, one from each tribe, to scout the land of Canaan, and they return with a glowing report of its fruitfulness but also warn that its inhabitants, including the intimidating descendants of Anak, are strong and the cities fortified. Only Caleb speaks up confidently that Israel can conquer the land, while the other spies' fearful report discourages the people.
chapters.14: Terrified by the spies' report, the people rebel, wishing to return to Egypt, and God threatens to destroy them, but Moses intercedes and God relents from wiping out the nation entirely. Instead, God decrees that this unbelieving generation will wander and die in the wilderness over forty years, with only Caleb and Joshua from that generation permitted to enter the promised land.
chapters.15: This chapter gives additional offering regulations, including grain and drink offerings to accompany sacrifices for both Israelites and foreigners, and a provision for atoning for unintentional communal and individual sins. It recounts the stoning of a man for deliberately breaking the Sabbath, and ends with the command to wear tassels with blue thread on garments as a reminder to keep God's commandments.
chapters.16: Korah, along with Dathan, Abiram, and 250 other leaders, rebels against Moses and Aaron's authority, challenging their exclusive leadership and priesthood. God dramatically vindicates Moses by having the earth swallow Korah's group and sending fire to consume the 250 rebels, and when the people complain afterward, a plague breaks out until Aaron intervenes to make atonement.
chapters.17: To settle who has God's authentic authority after Korah's rebellion, Moses collects a staff from each tribal leader, including one for Aaron representing Levi, and places them overnight in the tabernacle. In the morning, Aaron's staff alone has miraculously budded, blossomed, and produced almonds, confirming his priesthood and the staff is kept as a permanent sign against further rebellion.
chapters.18: God assigns Aaron and his fellow priests and the Levites responsibility for the sanctuary and its service, protecting the people from further consequences of approaching it improperly. In return, the priests and Levites are to receive their support from the people's offerings and tithes rather than from land inheritance, since God himself is their inheritance.
chapters.19: This chapter establishes the ritual of the red heifer, which is sacrificed and burned outside the camp, with its ashes mixed with water to create a purification mixture for anyone who becomes ceremonially unclean through contact with a dead body. It details how this "water of separation" is used and the waiting periods required to become clean again.
chapters.20: The people again complain about lacking water, and Moses strikes a rock to bring forth water, but because he and Aaron act without fully trusting God's instructions, both are told they will not enter the promised land. Later, Edom refuses to let Israel pass peacefully through its territory, and Aaron dies on Mount Hor, with his priestly garments transferred to his son Eleazar.
chapters.21: Israel defeats the Canaanite king of Arad, and after the people complain about the journey, God sends venomous snakes as judgment, relieved only when Moses makes a bronze serpent on a pole that heals those who look at it after being bitten. Israel then defeats Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, gaining control of territory east of the Jordan.
chapters.22: Balak, the king of Moab, alarmed by Israel's advance, sends for the prophet Balaam to curse Israel, but God tells Balaam not to go and then permits him to go only on the condition that he speaks only what God tells him. On the way, Balaam's donkey, seeing a blocking angel invisible to Balaam, refuses to proceed and miraculously speaks after Balaam strikes it, until Balaam himself finally sees the angel and is warned to speak only God's words.
chapters.23: Balaam offers sacrifices and, instead of cursing Israel as Balak wants, delivers a series of blessings on Israel under God's direction, declaring that Israel is blessed and that God does not lie or change his mind. A frustrated Balak repeatedly moves Balaam to new locations hoping for a different outcome, but Balaam insists he can only say what God puts in his mouth.
chapters.24: Balaam delivers a further series of blessings on Israel, including a famous prophecy of a coming "star out of Jacob" and ruler who will triumph over Israel's enemies, infuriating Balak, who sends him away without reward. Balaam also predicts the eventual downfall of several neighboring nations before returning home.
chapters.25: Israelite men begin sexual immorality with Moabite women and are drawn into worshiping the Moabite god Baal-peor, provoking God's anger and a deadly plague. Phinehas, grandson of Aaron, stops the plague by killing an Israelite man and a Midianite woman caught in the act, for which he is commended and given a covenant of perpetual priesthood.
chapters.26: Moses and Eleazar take a second census of the Israelite men of fighting age by tribe and clan as they prepare to enter Canaan, totaling 601,730, notably different individuals from the first census since that generation died in the wilderness. The chapter also notes Zelophehad's daughters, who had no brothers, and records the much smaller separate count of the Levites.
chapters.27: Zelophehad's daughters petition Moses for the right to inherit their deceased father's land since he had no sons, and God rules in their favor, establishing a precedent for daughters to inherit when there are no sons. Moses is then told he will not enter Canaan because of his earlier disobedience at the water of Meribah, and God designates Joshua as his successor to lead Israel.
chapters.28: This chapter outlines the required daily, weekly (Sabbath), and monthly burnt offerings and accompanying grain and drink offerings, and specifies the special offerings for Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, including the firstfruits offering.
chapters.29: This chapter continues the festival calendar with offerings for the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the seven-day Feast of Tabernacles, during which the number of bulls offered decreases by one each day, plus a closing eighth-day assembly.
chapters.30: This chapter sets rules for vows and oaths, especially those made by women, establishing that a father or husband has the authority to confirm or nullify a vow made by a daughter or wife if he objects when he first hears of it, while a widow's or divorced woman's vow stands on its own.
chapters.31: God commands Israel to take vengeance on the Midianites for leading them into the sin at Peor, and Israel's army kills the Midianite kings and all adult males, including Balaam, while taking captives and plunder. Moses then orders that most of the women be killed as well because of their role in the earlier idolatry, with the surviving plunder, including captive women and children, divided between the soldiers and the rest of the community after a purification process.
chapters.32: The tribes of Reuben and Gad ask to settle in the fertile grazing land east of the Jordan rather than cross into Canaan proper, which initially concerns Moses that they might discourage the rest of Israel as the earlier spies did. They agree to send their armed men to help conquer Canaan first before returning to their families, and Moses grants them and part of the tribe of Manasseh this eastern territory.
chapters.33: This chapter records the full list of campsites where Israel stopped during their forty years of wilderness wandering, from leaving Egypt to arriving at the plains of Moab. It ends with God's command to drive out all the inhabitants of Canaan and destroy their idols once Israel crosses the Jordan, warning that any people left behind will become a lasting source of trouble.
chapters.34: This chapter defines the exact borders of the promised land of Canaan that Israel is to inherit, describing its southern, western, northern, and eastern boundaries. It also names the leaders, including Eleazar and Joshua along with one appointed prince from each tribe, who will oversee dividing the land by lot.
chapters.35: God instructs that the Levites receive forty-eight cities with surrounding pasture land throughout Israel's territory rather than one large region, including six designated "cities of refuge" where someone who kills another person accidentally can flee for protection from revenge. It carefully distinguishes between intentional murder, which demands the death penalty, and accidental killing, which requires only staying in the city of refuge until the high priest's death.
chapters.36: The clan leaders of Manasseh raise a concern that if Zelophehad's daughters marry men from other tribes, their inherited land would transfer out of their own tribe, so God rules that such heiresses must marry within their father's tribe to keep the inheritance intact. The daughters comply by marrying their cousins, and the book closes by affirming these laws and regulations given to Israel through Moses in the plains of Moab.
